Shanghai Nov 20 1934
Dear Family:
Again I'm writing from the air - this time on a trip to
Chungking•
I left Shanghai this morning at 7.
We have one of those
rarest of phenomenons - a tail wind and made a fast trip to Nanking -
in fact we had to wait 10 minutes for the up river mail.
Our next
stop is Anking - then Klukiang and the end of this day's run at
Hankow. My fellow passengers are a Swede and two Chinese - one of
the latter Mr. Li was talking to me about his first trip in a plane
at Northampton, Mass. I told him that city was familiar territory
for me because I had gone to Amherst College - whereupon he put out
his hand and said "Shake, I'm an Amherst man too - class of 1927".
He said that he is the only Amherst graduate in Shanghai.
Wednesday Nov. 21st.
We arrived at 1.30 and Howard Norris
the pilot with the aid of Moleskey, one of the up river pilots
persuaded me to join them in a round of golf. I was surprised and
delighted to find that my arm did not bother me a bit and there 1s
no reason at all why I should not play as well (or as badly) as I
ever did.
My play in Hankow was unbelievably bad but my right arm
had nothing to do with the quality - or rather lack of quality - of
the golf I played.
The Hankow Club is reputed to be the best equip-
ped establishment of its kind in the Far East.
The club owns a traet
of 170 acres which was deeded to them years ago by the National
Government and some smart Scotohman - there are lots of Scots in
Hankow - got the Government to stipulate in the deed that taxes
the entire property should never be in excess of $22.00 Mex per annum
(about $7.00 U.S.)
Isn't it too bad that Dr. Beckers didn't make
a similar deal with the National Government of
Bolton Landing!
We are now approaching Ichang where we land to deliver mail
and then leaving Ichang we almost immediately start through the gorges
of the Yangtsze and I will then spend all of my time having a "look-see"
at the grandest scenery I have ever viewed, with the single exception
one trip which I made with lindbergh through the Canyon of the
In that flight we followed the river canyon for about 500
miles, occasionally going below the rim. Here the flight is only a
little over 100 miles and the gorges not as extensive as the Grand
Canyon nor as colorful - but entirely different.
Capt. Cornell Plant
who in 1900 pioneered steamboating on the upper reaches of the
Yangtze is authority for the statement that in the old days of ex-
clusive junk traftie before any dangerous rooks were blasted from the
channel that over 1000 men annually lost their lives in the rapids.
The waters of the Yangtze - a mile or more wide at points above and
below the gorges, are narrowed down to as little as 200 yards at
places where the solid rock clifts rise straight up on either side.
At these points the river has been known to rise 180 feet in 84 hours.
You can imagine the effect.
Later - Sunday Nov. 25th.
I arrived in Chungking Wednesday
afternoon at 3:30 p.m. and learned that Debby and the girls had arrived
early in the afternoon of the day before.
Called for them on their
boat and we all went up to the "May Foo"
or Standard 011 number one
residence for dinner.
Mr. and Mrs. Fitzsimmons (he was Yale "Shef"1916)
act as hosts to nearly all Amerioans who visit Chungking.
They live
on the opposite side of the river from Chungking on top of a hill
about the height of Shelving Rock at Lake George.
The girls were all
excited about the ride up in sedan chairs, their first experience with
that form of transport wakk vehicle.
Mr. Fitzsimmons had very tact-
fully suggested that I should order a four man chair for myself and
three man chairs for the girls - but he hadn't seen the girls!
all had four man chairs.

Debby drank two whiskey sodas before the start - and either on account
of that load of false courage or in spite of it - enjoyed the exper-
lence as did all the others.
There was some confusion at the Fitz-
simmons and our chairs were all sent back down so after dinner there
was nothering to do but walk down in the pitch dark.
We borrowed two
of Mr, Fitzsimmons boys with lanterns and made the descent without
any casualties.
It was exciting for Debby and the girls - me too -
walking through the several small wik villages so late at night.
following day we went over early to Chungking to do some shopping.
It was Debby's birthday and what a place for her to spend it!
Chungking the dirtiest most disorderly city in the world,
We bought
a lot of opium lamps - each of the girls bought a pipe and a lot of
other gadgets.
Poppies are still one of the stable crops in Szechuen
Province and it is about as hard to find a place to smoke opium as
it was to buy a drink in New York during probbition days.
Tew hours in Chungking we went back across the river and joined a
picnio party on a hike to the Asiatic Petroleum summer camp back on
the second range of mountains.
It was a long hard climb.
took a chair but the rest of us walked.
I regretted being scornful
of that chair many times and to tell the truth discovered that I*m
getting old. Just can't take it. The elimb was about equivalent to
Buok Mountain and wasn't so bad for the Chungking folks for they are
used to shagging those heights as a matter of daily routine - but for
us it was quite another matter coming from Shanghai where the highest
hill in the Garden Bridge over Boochow Creek which at the highest point
is 8 feet above sea level as contrasted with the general elevation
of 6 feet for the rest of Shanghai. Anyway we l1 ved through it and
the bottle of beer which I had at the camp was almost worth the
etrort, to say nothing of the view.
Our party consisted of some
traveling companions of Debby and the girls. Mr. and Mrs. Bragg who
are stationed at Chungking by the &.P.C., a Mr. Robinson whom Mr.
Bragg is sueceeding, a Dr. Wood off the U.S.S. Palos stationed at
Chungking and a very attractive young fellow who is the Standard 011
No. 2 man at Chungking•
We had a grand time and coming down stopped off for tea
with some old friends of mine Mr. and Irs. Holm. Postal Commissioner.
They have lived many years in China and Mrs. Holm with rare good taste
has collected a housefull of Chinese art objects which makes her
home the most attractive by far of any house I have seen in China.
The house is of Chinese architecture set amid a lovely garden over-
looking the Yangtze and the city of Chungking which is pioturesque
and interesting when sufficiently far away to be non-offensive to the
senses of eye, ear and nose. We had tea including the best cake you
have ever eaten plus a lavish supply of divinity candy, with the
result that the girls did fairly well toward restoring
went to the International Club where most all of the 30 foreign population
of Chungking had gathered to hear a lecture by Capt. Settle of the U.S.
in early as we were sailing early the next morning. The cook boy had
baked a birthday cake for Debby which looked poisonous on the outside
all decorated with red, green and yellow icing - but the inside was
I had arranged to take the boat as far as Wanhsien and fly
from there to Hankow as I want to be back in Shanghai Sunday. We
sailed at dawn and had a perfect day - bright sunshine.
I was pretty
well tired out as a result of several weeks of intensive work and just
relaxed in a steamer chair on the top deck. It was grand. We arrived
at Wanhsien that night and the following morning the boat sailed just
before dawn.
Arrangements
to have a sampan carry me
over to the CNAG
in the dakness I left the ship and entrusted

myself to three wioked looking boatmen in kx a large sampan.
They
promptly took me to the wrong place
and when I tried to direot them
in my very best Mandarin they couldn't get one word - guess they
talk another dialect.
Fortunately I knew about where
the CNAC
pontoon was located and eventually got there.
Whereupon they quite
obviously made it clear to me that they wanted more money than the
$1.00 agreed to for the trip.
They had been so stupid about under-
standing me that I thought it only polite to be equally stupid and
apparently succeeded for after 15 minutes of gestioulation and jab-
bering they departed in disgust leaving me all alone on the small
pontoon in the ghostlike half dusk, half dawn.
Wanhsien is reported
to be quite anti-foreign because of the "incident" which
there in 1927 when a British gunboat shelled the town.
took place
However
many boats went by with their trackers straining at the bamboo ropes
as they fought their tortous way up stream
and all seemed very friend-
ly when they might easily have been otherwise because I had no pro-
tection whatever. The plane came along on time and at 10:30 a.m.
I was on the way again through the gorges. A Chinese lady? passenger
dressed and painted to the limit was terribly 111 and Chili Vaughn
the pilot flew high so as to make the trip a smooth one.
We got up
about 5000 feet and passed the Wantung in the gorges looking 11ke
a toy down there in the rapids. Our trip was as smooth and the plane
as steady as any air trip I have ever made but the lady? was violently
111 all the way to Henkow and had to be carried out of the plane
when we landed.
Chili said she looked like she expected to meet
her
"maker" and I corrected him by suggesting the plural because I
felt convinced that several had "made her".
Chili Vaughn has an apartment in Hankow which he shares
with an Englishman. I stayed there last night and dined alone as
they both had engagements.
Then sat around reading the Sunday
New York Times which Chili subacribes to, until about 10:30.
a swell time. Up this morning at 6 and now at eleven o'elock we
are about an hour out of Nanking. The weather has been good but
our radio weather report at the last stop, inking, advised us that
Nanking is completely fog bound. Here we are in bright sunshine
but we can see the fog up ahead.
That's the advantage of a flying
boat - if the fog hasn't lifted we can land and taxi along the river
at 40 miles per hour or sit still if the fog 1s too thick and wait
for it to lift. Anyway there's nothing to worry about. Its funny
to watch the passengers. My companions in the cabin are one
American who is looking ahead at the fog bank, and two Chinese who
are both asleep. They may be too dumb to worry but I'm inclined to
think they are just smart in this respect as in most other respets.
There is nothing they can do about it - they have confidence in the
American pilot - so why worry when it will accomplish preeisely
nothing while a little "shut-eye" is always beneficial.
Later - Shortly after I wrote the above we were forced to
land on account of the fog.
You rarely find wind where there is fog
and today was no exception - so we taxied some five miles into
Nanking where we got a report that the weather was all right about
five miles east and so we took off and almost immediately ran into
sunshine and blue sky.
Now after being wway only 4} business days
I am again almost back to Shanghai.
Left Tuesday morning, played
18 holes of golf Tuesday afternoon at Hankow after covering 500 miles
left Hankow Wednesday morning and joined Debby and the giris Wednesday
afternoon. Had nearly as much time in Chungking as they did - all
day Thursday.
Friday on the boat to Wanhsien,
Saturday flying through
the gorges and today Sunday will arrive Shanghai at 1;30 in the after-
Debby and the girls left Shanghai Nov. 3rd and are scheduled
back again about Now. 30th.
You can see from that little story why
air transport has an important place in the future of this country.
The land in most parts of China is literally covered with a fine net
work of waterways providing the cheapest form of transportation.
